Changelog.html.body:
Change Log
All notable changes to this document will be documented in this file.
1.6.6
REST API

Update GET /auth/token and POST /auth/login - correct the 401 Unauthorized body; add 429 Too Many Requests and 503 Service Unavailable, which covers an OS account login too.
Update GET /edgehub/api/macaddr - add that the MAC is a default until one is recorded, and that a device credential for another network adapter changes it.
Update POST /edgehub/api/connection - replace the two conncfg examples with one of deviceTokenCredential, skipCertVerify and caCerts; add what a conncfg without deviceTokenCredential changes, what a failed connection clears, and that conncfg is refused as the body of POST /edgehub/api/conncfg is.
Update POST /edgehub/api/connection - add that "op": "connect" with conncfg enables the connection, which POST /edgehub/api/conncfg alone leaves disabled, and that AppHub has the device's MQTT connection only while the connection is enabled.
Update GET /edgehub/api/conncfg - document the response as a summary that holds no secret: add credential, type, x509 and certExpiresAt; remove password, overWebSocket, connectionString, deviceTokenCredential, iothubKey, iothubCert, mqttKey and mqttCert.
Update POST /edgehub/api/conncfg - replace the two request examples with one of deviceTokenCredential, skipCertVerify and caCerts, and describe each; add which MACs a device credential may be for, what happens when it names another adapter, and the 422 Unprocessable Entity for any other field; 200 OK now returns the summary, and 404 Not Found says when it applies.
Update POST /edgehub/api/conncfg - it stores the setting and leaves the connection disabled, also after a restart, until POST /edgehub/api/connection enables it; replace what a connected device does after a device credential for another adapter with when it takes that MAC.
Update POST /edgehub/api/data - add how the agent declares the tags it sends.
Update PUT /edgehub/api/apphub/service - add when the agent gives AppHub the device's MQTT connection and when it clears it with the certificate and key files, and that the agent restarts AppHub only to apply a change to its settings.
Update tls.skipVerify in GET /edgehub/api/provisioning/config - add what it means for skipCertVerify on a provisioned credential.
Update POST /edgehub/api/applications/provision - add the local channels that serve it and the account that owns each registration; replace the login in Request Headers with how the agent takes the caller's account; replace 401 Unauthorized with 403 Forbidden and its causes; extend 503 Service Unavailable.
Update GET /edgehub/api/wsl/status - reword accepted and keyRejected for relay keys the agent issues.
Update POST /edgehub/api/initialcode, Initial Code Retrieval, POST /edgehub/api/device/challenge and POST /edgehub/api/device/register - LAN onboarding is off by default and these answer 404 Not Found until it is turned on; the code field is broadcast only while the device has no stored connection configuration; the initial code unlocks only registering such a device, and stays the same until the service restarts or the device loses its configuration; add 409 Conflict for a device that has one.

CLI

Add the Data Directories page - where each service keeps its data, who may use it, and how to restrict a directory given with --config; list it in the table of contents.
Add a paragraph on running the service as root or as an administrator, with a link to Data Directories, to the auth-server, edgex-helper, portal-service and rest-server pages.
Add Failed logins to auth-server - the limits on failed logins, where to set them and how to unlock.
Update the rights paragraphs of edgehub-agent - add the app commands on Windows and the data directory on Linux, and link to Data Directories.
Add the app command to edgehub-agent - which account owns an application, the records the agent keeps, owners, assign and release, and their help text.
Add When an application is refused - what each reason means and what to do; list it in the table of contents.
Add LAN onboarding to edgehub-agent - the device.lanOnboarding setting, off by default, and how to turn it on; list it in the table of contents.
Update the conn command of edgehub-agent - remove --address, --port, --username, --password, --enable-tls, --over-ws and --cs from its help text, add rollback-key to it, and correct the --debug default; add where the device credential is set and what conn mac and conn mac --all print.
Update the wsl command of edgehub-agent - add the relay key setup installs, and that a container gets only an application the Windows user who set up the relay may have.
Name the program edgehub-agent.exe in the Windows-only text of edgehub-agent and of GET /edgehub/api/wsl/status.
Update --insecure-port in auth-server, edgehub-agent and rest-server - plain HTTP is off by default; reword its help text and add how to turn it on.
Update --address and --insecure-address in auth-server, edgehub-agent and rest-server - a blank address is 127.0.0.1, this host only; add to LAN onboarding and Initial Code Retrieval that the agent's HTTPS port listens on all interfaces only while it is on, and that a client on another host then reaches only the device challenge and registration there.
Update portal-service - remove the container command and the --container flag from its help text.
Update --max-refresh in auth-server - correct its default to 15m0s in the help text.

Dashboard

Update the EdgeHub widget - add that the stored Device Credential is kept when turning the connection on fails.
Update Device Credential - add the MACs a pasted Device Credential may be for, and the MAC logging in registers under.
Add Stored Device Credential - the summary shown for a stored Device Credential, REPLACE and CLEAR ALL, with two new screenshots.
Update SSL/TLS Connection - add changing the options of a stored Device Credential.
Update the Save Credential screenshots of Device Credential and SSL/TLS Connection.

Correct the Related REST APIs link of Application Monitor.

New Features

Add provisioning from containers in WSL 2 on Windows - a container that Docker or Podman runs in WSL 2 on a Windows device can provision an application credential through the EdgeHub agent, by way of a relay in its WSL distribution.

1.6.3
New Features

Add application provisioning - an application can register with the cloud under the device's identity and receive a credential of its own, through the EdgeHub agent.
Add POST /edgehub/api/applications/provision - register an application and return the credential the cloud issued. Provisioning is create-or-get: calling it again with the same name and type returns the same credential, so an application can call it on every start.



Fixes

Correct the EdgeHub entries in the table of contents: remove PUT /edgehub/api/bootstrap/config, whose endpoint was removed in 1.6.0; add the provisioning endpoints added in 1.6.0, which were documented but not listed; and remove a duplicated GET /edgehub/api/agentinfo. New Features

Add auto-provisioning flow (WISE2J NATS) - the EdgeHub agent now auto-provisions on first boot by exec'ing an external edgehub-bootstrap-provider binary and running a two-phase NATS exchange with the ASAN server. The resulting device credential is stored in the existing device.cs slot and the agent proceeds to MQTT connect as usual.
Add GET /edgehub/api/provisioning/config - query the provisioning configuration.
Add PUT /edgehub/api/provisioning/config - update the provisioning configuration.
Add POST /edgehub/api/provisioning/reprovision - re-run the auto-provisioning flow on demand (non-blocking; returns 202 Accepted, or 409 Conflict when a run is already active).


Add "Provisioning" tab in EdgeHub agent settings UI with a "Run provisioning now" action for operators to retry after fixing a misconfigured provider path or recovering from a transient network issue.

Dashboard.html.title: Dashboard
Dashboard.html.body:
Dashboard
The Dashboard summarizes system information and provides an EdgeHub widget.

EdgeHub
This widget enables and disables the connection to the cloud, MQTT/Azure IoTHub connection settings. If turning the connection on fails, for example while the network is down, the stored Device Credential is kept; turn the connection on again later.

Device Credential

You could follow the hint to copy the Device Credential or Login to EdgeHub to get the Device Credential automatically.


Copy Credential and Paste Credential
Click the "Copy Credential" button on the "Connection" tab of a device on the EdgeHub and then click the "Paste Credential" button to paste the credential to the "Device Credential" textarea (or by Ctrl+V).

A Device Credential issued for the MAC of any of the device's wired or wireless network adapters is accepted, also in place of a stored one, so the device may be registered on EdgeHub under any of them; the device then uses that MAC, and the MAC shown in the widget changes to it. The agent checks this when you click SAVE, and reports a Device Credential for a MAC that is not one of the device's adapters as device ID mismatch; see POST /edgehub/api/conncfg.

Login to Credential
Logging in registers the device under the MAC shown in the widget. To use a device created on EdgeHub by hand under the MAC of another adapter, paste its Device Credential instead. If the device's MAC changed while the dialog was open, for example because a Device Credential for another adapter was saved in another session, logging in stops before it registers the device and shows the new MAC; log in again.
1. Log in with your EdgeHub account.

2. Enter the verification code if two-factor authentication is enabled for your EdgeHub account.

3. Select a tenant if required



Now, you can click the SAVE button to apply the Device Credential to your device.
  
Stored Device Credential
Once a Device Credential is stored, the Connection Setting tab shows a summary of it instead of the textarea: the device type, MAC and UUID, the broker (marked (TLS) when the connection is encrypted), the username when there is one, how the device authenticates (X.509 certificate, or username and password) and, for an X.509 credential, when its client certificate expires (marked (expired) once it has). The credential itself, with its password and private keys, is never shown again.
  

Replace Device Credential
Click the REPLACE button to paste a new Device Credential. The textarea and the Paste Credential button come back with a note that saving replaces the stored Device Credential: click the SAVE button to replace it, or CANCEL to keep the stored one.


Logging in on the Login EdgeHub tab also replaces the stored Device Credential.

Click the CLEAR ALL button to remove it from the device.

SSL/TLS Connection
The agent enables the SSL/TLS connection to the EdgeHub server by default. But for the servers that do not have valid certificates (i.e. self-signed, using IP for the server), you could add the extra CA certificates or skip the certificate verification by disabling the Secure SSL/TLS.
These options stay editable after a Device Credential is stored: change them and click SAVE to apply them to the stored credential without pasting it again. Each CA certificate must be in PEM format and hold certificates only; anything else is refused. If the connection fails with the new options, they stay stored along with the credential, so change them again to fix it. Secure SSL/TLS keeps the value set here, also when the cloud rotates the credential.
  
Provisioning
(since 1.7.0)
Provisioning automates device onboarding by exec'ing a local edgehub-bootstrap-provider binary to obtain bootstrap credentials at startup, and then uses those credentials to fetch the long-lived device credential from the platform. Each device vendor ships their own provider implementation, so the agent does not need to know where the bootstrap material is stored (TPM, encrypted file, secure enclave, etc.).

Configuration:

Provider binary path — absolute path to the edgehub-bootstrap-provider executable. Leave empty to look the binary up on PATH.
Provider timeout — how long to wait for the provider binary to return bootstrap credentials (e.g. 10s, 30s).
Max retries — number of retry attempts for the provisioning exchange before giving up.
Secure SSL/TLS — enable TLS server certificate verification during provisioning. Disable (dev/test only) for servers with self-signed or invalid certificates.

Actions:

SAVE — persist the configuration. New values apply on the next provisioning run.
RUN PROVISIONING NOW — re-run the auto-provisioning flow on demand. Useful after fixing a misconfigured provider path, recovering from a transient network failure, or rotating device credentials.

Notes:

If the edgehub-bootstrap-provider binary is not installed on the device, the agent remains in a disconnected idle state until the binary is installed and provisioning is retriggered.
Provisioning runs asynchronously. Watch the connection status on the EdgeHub Dashboard widget for progress.

EdgeX/modbus.html.title: Modbus (Downlink)
EdgeX/modbus.html.body:
Modbus
This page describes how to connect Modbus devices to EdgeX. In this example, we simulate the Advantech WISE-4220-S231 (2.4G WiFi IoT Wireless Module with Temperature & Humidity Sensor)  instead of using a real device. This provides a straightforward way to test the device service features.
For more detail information to setup EdgeX Modbus, it might reference to
https://docs.edgexfoundry.org/2.0/examples/Ch-ExamplesAddingModbusDevice/
Modbus entity Number and Address
It is important to make a distinction between Modbus entity number and entity address:

Entity numbers combine entity type and entity location within their description table.
Entity address is the starting address, a 16-bit value in the data part of the Modbus frame. As such its range goes from 0 to 65,535 (0000 to FFFF in the packets)

In the traditional conventio, entity numbers start with a single digit representing the entity type, followed by four digits representing the entity location:

coils numbers start with 0 and span from 00001 to 09999,
discrete input numbers start with 1 and span from 10001 to 19999,
input register numbers start with 3 and span from 30001 to 39999,
holding register numbers start with 4 and span from 40001 to 49999.

For data communications, the entity location number (1 to 9,999) is translated into a 0-based entity address (0 to 9,998) by subtracting 1. For example, for holding registers starting at number 40100, address (starting address) will be 99 etc.
For more detail information about the Modbus protocol, it might reference to Coil, discrete input, input register, holding register numbers and addresses
Modbus Register Table

3.isByteSwap, isWordSwap: To handle the different Modbus binary data order, we support Int32, Uint32, Float32 to do the swap operation before decoding the binary data.
For example: { primaryTable: "INPUT_REGISTERS", startingAddress: "4", isByteSwap: "false", isWordSwap: "true" }
4.rawType: This attribute defines the binary data read from the Modbus device, then we can use the value type to indicate the data type that the user wants to receive.
We only support Int16 and Uint16 for rawType. The corresponding value type must be Float32 and Float64.

specifies that a value has two registers, define it as Float32 or Int32

register type, startingAddress, and register length. So it can read or

GET /auth/token{?m}
Get with the OS or the admin account and return a JWT token if the user is valid.
A request contains a header field in the form of Authorization: Basic , where credentials is the Base64 encoding of username and password joined by a single colon :
username:password => (base64) => dXNlcm5hbWU6cGFzc3dvcmQ=
(since v1.7.1, API version 1.1)

URI Parameters
m number (optional) - User account type. (since v1.8.1, API version 1.2)

2: admin account (default password: p@ssw0rd, must be changed after login)


Request Header

Login Successfully

  "token": ""
}


Cookie (if available)
Secure and HttpOnly cookies
Key: jwt
Value: 




Response 401 Unauthorized
Login Failed. The answer is the same for an unknown username and a wrong password, on every account type. A request without a username and a password also answers 401, with a message that says what is missing.
{
    "code": 401,
    "message": "incorrect Username or Password"
}


Response 429 Too Many Requests
Too many failed logins in a row with this username and account type, so the password was not checked. A login sent while as many others with this username are still being checked as it has attempts left gets this answer too, for one second. The answer is the same for every username and password, whether or not the account exists. Retry-After gives the seconds to wait. Failed logins gives the limits and how to unlock.
Retry-After: 300

{
    "code": 429,
    "message": "too many failed logins, try again later"
}


Response 503 Service Unavailable
The login could not be checked, as when the OS cannot reach a logon server, the LDAP server cannot be reached or the LDAP configuration is not valid. This does not say that the username or the password is wrong, and it does not count as a failed login. The answer gives no reason; the auth-server logs it.
{
    "code": 503,
    "message": "authentication service unavailable"
}

POST /edgehub/api/conncfg
Set the connection setting and disable the connection.
The device disconnects and stays disconnected, also after a restart, until POST /edgehub/api/connection with "op": "connect" enables the connection (since edgehub-agent 2.4.0); before, it set the connection enabled, and the device connected at its next start. A device can so hold a device credential for an EdgeHub it cannot reach yet, such as one stored on a production line and enabled on site.

Request Headers
Log in with the OS or the "admin" account to get a JWT token (token field from the response body).

Request Body

    "deviceTokenCredential": "", // optional (since edgehub-agent 2.4.0)

}


deviceTokenCredential: The device credential copied from EdgeHub, base64-encoded; it replaces the stored one. Without it, the stored device credential is kept and only skipCertVerify and caCerts change, and skipCertVerify must then be given.
The device credential has to be for this device: for the MAC GET /edgehub/api/macaddr returns, or for the MAC of any of its wired or wireless network adapters; on Windows an adapter whose MAC is overridden also counts by its burned-in MAC. A virtual interface, such as a bridge, a veth pair or a tunnel, is not a network adapter here. A device credential for another of its adapters, also in place of a stored one, moves the device to that MAC: GET /edgehub/api/macaddr returns it from then on, POST /edgehub/api/device/register and automatic provisioning register under it, and the cloud device registered under the previous MAC is no longer used (since edgehub-agent 2.4.0). A device credential for any other MAC is refused with 422 Unprocessable Entity and a message that starts with device ID mismatch.

skipCertVerify: Skip verifying the server's certificate chain and host name.
caCerts: Extra CA certificates to trust, each a base64-encoded PEM holding certificates only. They replace the stored ones; an entry that is anything else is refused with 422 Unprocessable Entity, and nothing is changed.

These are the only fields accepted (since edgehub-agent 2.4.0): a body with any other field, among them the fields of the earlier format such as username, password, mqttHost, mqttPort, enableTLS, overWebSocket, connectionString, mac or uuid, is refused with 422 Unprocessable Entity.

POST /edgehub/api/applications/provision
Register an application with the cloud under this device's identity, and return the credential the cloud issued for it. (since edgehub-agent 2.4.0)
An application credential is an identity of its own, separate from the device's: it carries its own devId and uuid and isApp: true, and shares the device's mac. The agent obtains it on the device's behalf and does not keep a copy; what the caller does with it is the caller's responsibility.
The agent serves this request only on its local channels, where it can tell which operating system account is calling: the application pipe \\.\pipe\edgehub_app on Windows and /run/edgehub/app.sock on Linux, which every local user may open, and the agent's own pipe or socket, which only administrators and SYSTEM, or root, may open. Over HTTP or HTTPS it answers 401 Unauthorized without a login and 403 Forbidden with one. Applications running on the device normally obtain their credential through the EdgeHub Connect SDK.
Provisioning is create-or-get, and each registration belongs to one account. If the name is already registered for this device and type, the account that owns the registration receives the existing credential rather than an error, so an application can call this on every start with the same name and receive the same credential each time. The owner is the account whose request made the cloud register the application, or, for a registration the cloud already had and no account on the device owned, the first account that asked for it. A container counts as the account that runs its container engine. Any other account is refused. Two programs of one account that pick the same name share one identity; for an Application (type 3) the agent logs a warning whenever it returns an existing registration. An administrator changes owners with the edgehub-agent app command.

Request Headers
None. The agent takes the caller's account from the local channel: on Windows from the pipe client, which has to open the pipe at the SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION impersonation level or above, and on Linux from the socket's peer credentials.

Request Body
{
    "type": 3,
    "appName": "Line 3 Sensor",
    "timeoutMs": 60000,
    "x509": 1
}


type (required): The application type: 1 EdgeLink, 2 SCADA, 3 Application.
appName (required): The application name, following the rules below.
timeoutMs (optional): How long the agent may spend on the request, in milliseconds. Absent, zero or negative means the default, 60000; values above 300000 are capped there. A new registration usually takes a few seconds, so a value of a few seconds or less may expire before the cloud answers.
x509 (optional): Whether the credential includes client certificates: 1 yes, 0 no. Absent means 1, except for SCADA (type 2), which defaults to 0.


Application Name Rules
A name is accepted when it

is 1 to 32 characters long,
is made of letters and digits in any script, combining marks, and the separators -, _ and space,
contains at least one letter or digit,
neither starts nor ends with a separator, and has no two separators in a row, and
writes every character in its standard form: full-width Latin such as Ｓｅｎｓｏｒ and half-width katakana such as ｾﾝｻｰ are refused, while Sensor and センサー are accepted.

Emoji, punctuation such as . and /, and invisible characters are refused. Leading and trailing spaces are not trimmed; they are refused like any other separator at either end.
Names are compared without regard to case: Sensor01 and sensor01 are one application. The same name can be registered once for each type. EdgeLink and SCADA are reserved for types 1 and 2, and cannot be used as the name of a type 3 application.

Response 200 OK
{
    "credentialString": "{\"devId\":12345,\"name\":\"Line 3 Sensor\",\"isApp\":true,\"type\":\"Application\",\"uuid\":\"00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000\",\"mac\":\"001122AABBCC\", ...}"
}


credentialString: The credential exactly as the cloud issued it: a JSON document, encoded as a string. Parse it as JSON. The agent does not reshape it, so fields the cloud adds later pass through unchanged.

When x509 is 0, the credential's x509 object holds only ca, revokeUrl and status. The certificate and key fields are absent, not empty.

Response 403 Forbidden
The caller may not have this application, and asking again will not change that: the registration belongs to another account on the device; a container asked for an application other than the one its labels name, or has no labels; a container reached the agent's own socket instead of /run/edgehub/app.sock; on Linux, the calling account has a user ID from 61184 to 65519, which can own no application because systemd gives that range to services with DynamicUser=yes, so the application, or the engine of its container, has to run as a user outside that range; the agent found out something about the caller that keeps it from telling which account is calling, as when a Windows program opened the pipe anonymously, or a Linux caller is in a container of a runtime the agent does not know; or the request did not come through the agent's local channels. When an application is refused says what to do for each.
{
    "message": "SCADA \"plant-a\": the application belongs to another account on this device"
}


Response 422 Unprocessable Entity
The request itself is wrong and will be refused again as it stands: a malformed body, an unknown type, an unacceptable appName, or an undefined x509 mode. Change the request before sending it again.
{
    "message": "invalid application name: \"Sensor.01\" contains U+002E, which is not a letter, a digit, a combining mark, or one of the separators '-' '_' and space (CHAR:U+002E)"
}

When the name breaks one of the rules above, the message ends with the rule's identifier in parentheses, which is stable and safe to match on: LENGTH:, COMPAT:U+XXXX, CHAR:U+XXXX, NO_LETTER_OR_DIGIT or SEPARATOR_PLACEMENT. A reserved name is refused without one, as invalid application name: "EdgeLink" is reserved for another application type.

Response 502 Bad Gateway
The cloud answered and refused, or answered in a form the agent could not read. The message carries the cloud's reason, for example APP_INVALID_X509. Sending the same request again will not change the answer.

Response 503 Service Unavailable
The agent could not do the work, and nothing about the request was wrong: it is not connected to the cloud yet, which is normal for a short while after it starts; it is shutting down; it failed to identify the caller, as when the caller exited while the agent read it, and the message names what failed; its connection to the cloud changed during the request; the cloud never answered; or it cannot read or write its records of which account owns which application, or make sure a change to them reached the disk; its log names the file, and an administrator repairs or removes a file that cannot be read, and restarts the agent. Retry. Retrying is safe: provisioning is create-or-get, so a later attempt returns whatever an earlier one registered, and a registration made by a request that got no answer goes to the first account that asks for it, normally the one retrying.

Response 504 Gateway Timeout
The request ran out of time before the cloud answered. The registration may or may not have been made; retrying with the same name is safe for the same reason.


GET /edgehub/api/wsl/status
Get what the agent sees of the relays through which containers in WSL 2 reach it on a Windows device: the WSL virtual machines it listens on, and the connections that came through each. (since edgehub-agent 2.4.0)
A relay is installed in each WSL distribution that runs a container engine, with the edgehub-agent.exe wsl setup command. The WSL distributions of one Windows user share one virtual machine, so this endpoint reports per virtual machine, not per distribution; to check the relay in one distribution, run edgehub-agent.exe wsl status --distro  on the device. The counts start from zero when the agent starts.

Request Headers
Log in with the OS or the "admin" account to get a JWT token (token field from the response body).
Authorization: Bearer 


Response 200 OK
{
    "port": 20058,
    "listedAt": "2026-09-30T15:06:52.8747547+08:00",
    "vms": [
        {
            "id": "9238e7c9-9f94-432c-bc96-87e5fb7169ad",
            "listening": true,
            "accepted": 5,
            "keyRejected": 0,
            "badPreamble": 0,
            "capRejected": 0,
            "live": 0,
            "lastRelay": "2026-09-30T14:48:55.5280457+08:00",
            "relayVersion": "v2.4.0"

Times are in RFC 3339 format, in the device's local time.

port: The Hyper-V socket (vsock) port the agent listens on for each WSL virtual machine, to which the relays connect. It is not a TCP port.
listError (optional): Why the agent's last attempt to list the running WSL virtual machines failed. The listeners it already has stay open meanwhile. On a device without WSL 2 this stays set, and vms stays empty.

skippedOwners (optional): The owners of the other Hyper-V compute systems found in the last listing, which are not WSL virtual machines and which the agent does not listen on.

listening: Whether the agent is listening on the virtual machine.
listenError (optional): Why the agent could not listen, while listening is false. The agent keeps retrying.
accepted: Connections accepted from a relay that presented a relay key the agent issued.
keyRejected: Connections refused because the relay presented no key the agent issued: one set up by an earlier agent, or one whose key the agent no longer has. Run edgehub-agent.exe wsl setup again for its distribution.
badPreamble: Connections refused because the relay's opening message could not be read.
capRejected: Connections refused because a limit on open connections was reached, for one container, for the virtual machine, or for the agent as a whole.
live: Connections open now.
lastRelay (optional): When the last connection was accepted. Absent until one is.
relayVersion (optional): The version of the relay that made the last accepted connection.

The agent serves no WSL relay: it is not running on Windows, or it could not load its relay key, and its log says why. An agent older than 2.4.0 answers the same.

{

POST /edgehub/api/initialcode
Retrieve the current initial code for device registration. This endpoint exists only while LAN onboarding is on; otherwise it answers 404 Not Found. See Initial Code Retrieval.

Request Headers
To access this endpoint, log in with an OS or "admin" account to obtain a JWT token (token field in the response body). Include the token in the request header.
Authorization: Bearer 


Response 200 OK
{
    "code": "9c46e07d81d247614cfb053bca94c45080b52086d425728aa88ba338b1cdd453"
}


code: The current initial code for the device registration process. It stays the same until the service restarts or the device loses its stored connection configuration.



Initial Code Retrieval
LAN onboarding, which registers a device from the local network with an initial code, is off by default. While it is off, the device does not advertise itself over mDNS and has no initial code, and POST /edgehub/api/initialcode, POST /edgehub/api/device/challenge and POST /edgehub/api/device/register answer 404 Not Found. LAN onboarding tells how to turn it on.
While LAN onboarding is on, the initial code required for device registration can be retrieved by either of the following methods:

mDNS Browsing:

The device advertises the service name _edgehub._tcp.local. over the local network via mDNS whether it has a stored connection configuration or not, so clients can list every device by browsing it.
The initial code is broadcasted only while the device has no stored connection configuration. To retrieve it, clients can filter the TXT record, where the code field appears as code=. A device with a stored connection configuration has no code field.
This method is suitable for trusted internal networks where mDNS broadcasts are accessible, and it allows clients to dynamically discover the initial code without direct API access.


REST API Request:

Alternatively, clients can retrieve the initial code using the POST /edgehub/api/initialcode endpoint, which requires authorization via a JWT token obtained through login.
This approach provides direct access to the latest initial code when mDNS may not be available or accessible.



These options allow clients flexibility in retrieving the initial code based on network availability and security requirements.
The initial code unlocks one thing: registering a device that has no stored connection configuration, through POST /edgehub/api/device/challenge and POST /edgehub/api/device/register. Every other route requires a JWT token, and a client on another host that reaches the agent's own HTTPS port instead of the portal gets 403 Forbidden on it, as LAN onboarding describes. Anyone who can hear the mDNS broadcast can register such a device, so keep a device that is not yet registered on a trusted network.
POST /edgehub/api/device/challenge
Initiate a device challenge by generating a key that authenticates the request. This endpoint exists only while LAN onboarding is on; otherwise it answers 404 Not Found. See Initial Code Retrieval.

Request Headers
This request does not require JWT-based authorization, as it relies on a challenge-response authentication mechanism.

Request Body
{
    "clientID": "",  // Unique identifier generated by the client
    "key": ""        // HMAC and bcrypt-derived hash
}


clientID: A unique identifier generated by the client. This value is combined with an initial code (server-generated) to create a key.
key: A hashed value used to verify the client. The key is generated by combining clientID and initial code using HMAC and bcrypt.


Key Generation Process
To generate the key, the client combines its unique clientID and the server-provided initial code (which can be obtained via mDNS or by calling POST /edgehub/api/initialcode). Here's the process in detail:

Concatenate clientID and initial code into a single string.
Generate an HMAC using SHA-256, with the initial code as the secret key and the concatenated string as the data.
Hash the HMAC result with SHA-256 to ensure no NULL bytes are included, producing a consistent output for bcrypt.
Hash the SHA-256 result using bcrypt to produce a secure, one-way key value.
Convert the bcrypt result to a hex string to get the final key.


Note: This approach ensures the key is unique and valid only while the initial code is active.

Example in Golang:
func GenerateKey(initialCode, clientID string) (string, error) {
  data := fmt.Sprintf("%s%s", clientID, initialCode)
  h := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(initialCode))
  h.Write([]byte(data))
  hmacResult := h.Sum(nil)

  // Hash the HMAC result with SHA-256 to ensure no NULL bytes are included.
  sha256Result := sha256.Sum256(hmacResult)

  // Generate bcrypt hash from SHA-256 result.
  bcryptHash, err := bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword(sha256Result[:], bcrypt.DefaultCost)

  if err != nil {
    return "", err
  }

  return hex.EncodeToString(bcryptHash), nil
}


Response 200 OK
{
    "code": ""  // A new code for the client to use in subsequent requests
}


code: A server-generated code for continued access, stored for clientID and used for /api/device/register requests.


Response 400 Bad Request
{
    "message": ""
}

This error occurs if the clientID or key is not found or is invalid.

Response 401 Unauthorized
{
    "message": "Unauthorized"
}

This error occurs if the key validation fails.


POST /edgehub/api/device/register
Complete the device registration process with clientID, code, and additional registration details.
The device will connect to the EdgeHub once the registration process is successful.
This registers a device that has no stored connection configuration; see 409 Conflict below. This endpoint exists only while LAN onboarding is on; otherwise it answers 404 Not Found. See Initial Code Retrieval.

Request Headers
No JWT-based authorization is required for this endpoint, as it uses the challenge-response mechanism for validation.

Request Body
{
    "clientID": "UKmEjSdv6Apcz4fC",
    "code": "d38c58c86d1dc04a0723940cb767454c45da3f54877d92c5b91aec7420417657",
    "timestamp": 1730158176,

    "baseUrl": "https://api-dm-center-master-ensaas.edge365.advantech.com/v1.1",
    "orgId": 10,
    "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzUxMiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
}


clientID: Unique identifier generated by the client.
code: Generated response code based on the challenge code and timestamp provided during the challenge-response process.
timestamp: The current client-side time when generating code.

Additional Registration Fields:

baseUrl: The base URL for the device management API, selected from the station list.

https://bi.wise-deviceon.advantech.com/api/stationList
https://wise-deviceon-bi.azurewebsites.net/api/stationList
Within each station's data, the url_apidm field represents the possible baseUrl values. For example:
{
    "stationList": [
        {
            "name": "EdgeSync360/EdgeHub Master Station",
            "url": "https://pivot-api-hub-master-ensaas.edge365.advantech.com",
            "url_apidm": "https://api-dm-center-master-ensaas.edge365.advantech.com/v1.1"
        }
    ]
}




orgId: Organization ID from the selected tenant's organization data. This value is retrieved from the tenant array in the {baseUrl}/connect/login response.

token: JWT access token obtained from the {baseUrl}/connect/login response. The accessToken field in the response body represents this token.


Code Generation Process
The client generates code as follows:

Concatenate clientID, challenge code, and timestamp into a single string.
Generate an HMAC using SHA-256 with the initial code as the secret key and the concatenated string as data.
Convert the HMAC result to a hex string to produce the final code.

Example in Golang:
func GenerateResponseCode(initialCode, clientID, challengeCode string, timestamp int64) string {
    data := fmt.Sprintf("%s%s%d", clientID, challengeCode, timestamp)
    h := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(initialCode))
    h.Write([]byte(data))
    return hex.EncodeToString(h.Sum(nil))
}


Response 200 OK
{
    "message": "Device registered successfully",
}


Response 400 Bad Request
{
    "message": ""
}

This error occurs if the baseUrl, orgId or the token is not found or is invalid.

Response 401 Unauthorized
{
    "message": ""
}

This error occurs if the code validation fails.

Response 409 Conflict
{
    "message": ""
}

This error occurs if the code is valid and the device already has a stored connection configuration, including one it keeps because it cannot use it. Nothing is sent to EdgeHub and the stored configuration is not changed. To register the device again, first remove the stored configuration with DELETE /edgehub/api/conncfg.

Response 500 Internal Server Error
{
    "message": ""
}

This error occurs if device registration or onboarding fails.

cli/datadir.html.title: Data Directories
cli/datadir.html.body:
Data Directories
Each Edge Suite service keeps its configuration in a data directory of its own, and most of them their keys and certificates as well:



Service
Windows
Linux




auth-server
C:\ProgramData\Advantech\.auth-server
/etc/xdg/Advantech/.auth-server


edgehub-agent
C:\ProgramData\Advantech\.edgehub-agent
/etc/xdg/Advantech/.edgehub-agent


edgex-helper
C:\ProgramData\Advantech\.edgex-helper
/etc/xdg/Advantech/.edgex-helper


portal-service
C:\ProgramData\Advantech\.portal-service
/etc/xdg/Advantech/.portal-service


rest-server
C:\ProgramData\Advantech\.rest-server
/etc/xdg/Advantech/.rest-server



On Linux the directories are under the first entry of XDG_CONFIG_DIRS when that variable is set.
Who may use them
A data directory holds secrets, among them the device credential, encrypted under a key derived from the machine ID, which every local account can read. Whoever can read the directory can therefore read the secrets, and whoever can change it can change the service's configuration and keys. So a service started as an administrator, SYSTEM or root keeps its data directory to itself:

On Windows, the directory lets in only administrators and SYSTEM, and everything in it takes that rule unless an administrator gave an item rules of its own. At start, the service renames anything there that neither SYSTEM nor the Administrators group owns to name.untrusted-time, and creates what it needs anew.
On Linux, the directory belongs to root and has mode 0700, so no other account can list it or read the files in it. A directory an earlier version left open is closed the next time its service starts. One on a read-only file system cannot be closed: the service logs a warning that any account may read it, and does not stop for that reason; it still stops if it needs to write a file there, such as an HTTPS certificate it has not made yet.

Run the services and their commands as root on Linux, for example with sudo, and from a command prompt opened with Run as administrator on Windows. The commands of an ordinary user cannot read the data directory: the edgehub-agent commands that need it say so and stop (on Windows, some of them run in an ordinary command prompt, see edgehub-agent), and every command of the other services, --help and --version included, fails with unable to load HTTPS server certificate.
A directory given with --config
--config moves a service's data directory elsewhere. The service leaves a directory given this way as it is, and, started as an administrator or root, refuses to start while an account other than SYSTEM and Administrators on Windows, or root on Linux, owns the directory or anything in it, or may read or change it, or while anything in it is a symbolic link or a junction; replace a link with what it points to. The error names the first item that fails and gives the commands that restrict the directory. A directory that does not exist yet is created for the service alone, together with any missing directory above it, once the directories above it pass.
The commands give everything in the directory to the service, so do not give --config a directory that other software uses as well. They do not close a file that another account already holds open: if one may have, restart the device before starting the service, or use a new directory instead.
On Linux, where the second command also closes every file in the directory to other accounts, which could otherwise reach a file through a hard link made elsewhere:
sudo chown -R root:root /path/to/dir && sudo chmod -R go-rwx /path/to/dir

On Windows, from a PowerShell opened with Run as administrator, writing a ' in the path as '':
icacls 'C:\path\to\dir' /setowner *S-1-5-32-544 /T /C
icacls 'C:\path\to\dir' /reset /T /C
icacls 'C:\path\to\dir' /inheritance:r /grant:r '*S-1-5-18:(OI)(CI)F' '*S-1-5-32-544:(OI)(CI)F'

The first command makes the Administrators group the owner of the directory and everything in it, the second drops every access rule set on them so that they only take the rules of the folders above, and the third leaves the directory itself only rules that give SYSTEM and Administrators full control, which everything in it then takes.
A service also refuses a directory while such an account may change a directory above it, as that account could then put a directory of its own in its place. On Linux, every directory above must belong to root and let no other account write to it, unless it has the sticky bit, as /tmp has; on Windows, every folder above must belong to SYSTEM, Administrators or TrustedInstaller and let no other account delete or rename it or what it holds. The error names the directory above that fails; no command is given for it, so choose another place. A directory directly under C:\ or in C:\ProgramData meets this; one in a user's profile or home directory does not.

cli/authserver.html.title: Advantech JWT Authentication Service (CLI)
cli/authserver.html.body:
Advantech JWT Authentication Service (CLI)
Usage:
  auth-server [flags]
  auth-server [command]

Available Commands:
  help        Help about any command
  ldap        setup the LDAP authentication
  password    Manage admin password
  service     Manage service

Flags:
  -a, --address string                The IP address on which to listen for the --port port.
                                      If blank, 127.0.0.1: this host only. Set to 0.0.0.0 for all IPv4
                                      interfaces and :: for all IPv6 interfaces.
  -p, --port int                      The port on which to serve HTTPS with
                                      authentication and authorization.
                                      (default 6443)
      --tls-cert-file string          File containing the default x509 Certificate for HTTPS.
                                      (CA cert, if any, concatenated after server cert).
                                      If --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file are not provided,
                                      a self-signed certificate and key are generated for the public address
                                      and saved to the --tls-key-dir.
                                       (default "cert.crt")
      --tls-private-key-file string   File containing the default x509 private key
                                      matching --tls-cert-file.
                                       (default "key.pem")
      --tls-key-dir string            Location of --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file
                                       (default "/etc/xdg/Advantech/.auth-server/keys")
      --insecure-address string       The IP address on which to serve the --insecure-port.
                                      If blank, 127.0.0.1: this host only. Set to 0.0.0.0 for all IPv4
                                      interfaces and :: for all IPv6 interfaces.
      --insecure-port int             The port on which to serve plain HTTP, which does not encrypt
                                      passwords or tokens. Off by default. Set to 0 to disable.
      --jwt-cert-file string          File containing the default x509 Certificate for JWT.
                                      (CA cert, if any, concatenated after server cert).
                                      If --jwt-cert-file and --jwt-private-key-file are not provided,
                                      a self-signed certificate and key are generated for the public address
                                      and saved to the --jwt-key-dir.
                                       (default "cert.crt")
      --jwt-private-key-file string   File containing the default x509 private key matching --jwt-cert-file.
                                       (default "key.pem")
      --jwt-key-dir string            Location of --jwt-cert-file and --jwt-private-key-file
                                       (default "/etc/xdg/Advantech/.auth-server/jwt/keys")
      --timeout duration              Duration that a jwt token is valid. (default 15m0s)
      --max-refresh duration          It allows clients to refresh their token until --max-refresh has passed.
                                      Note that clients can refresh their token in the last moment of --max-refresh.
                                      This means that the maximum validity timespan for a token is
                                       --timeout + --max-refresh. Set to 0 to disable. (default 15m0s)
      --jwt-secure-cookie             Return the token as a cookie with Secure and HttpOnly flags (default true)
  -d, --debug                         enable debug output (default disabled)
      --config string                 Location of config files (default /etc/xdg/Advantech/.auth-server)
  -h, --help                          help for auth-server
      --version                       version for auth-server

Use "auth-server [command] --help" for more information about a command.

Run auth-server as root on Linux, for example with sudo, and from a command prompt opened with Run as administrator on Windows: as any other user it cannot read its data directory, and every command, --help and --version included, fails with unable to load HTTPS server certificate. Data Directories also tells how to restrict a directory given with --config, which auth-server refuses to start on otherwise.
Plain HTTP is off by default. To turn it on, give --insecure-port, or server.http.port in the config file, a port other than 6880: that was its default, and it now turns plain HTTP off. The exception is a device with HTTPS off (server.https.port 0), where that port stays on, because a service must keep one of the two.

service command
Manage service

Usage:
  auth-server service [flags]
  auth-server service [command]

Available Commands:
  install     install service
  restart     restart service
  start       start service
  stop        stop service
  uninstall   uninstall service

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for service

Global Flags:
      --config string   Location of config files (default /etc/xdg/Advantech/.auth-server)

Use "auth-server service [command] --help" for more information about a command.


password command
Manage admin password

Usage:
  auth-server password [flags]
  auth-server password [command]

Available Commands:
  reset       reset admin password

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for password

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

Use "auth-server password [command] --help" for more information about a command.



Failed logins
After 3 failed logins in a row with one username, that username is locked for 5 minutes: every login with it answers 429 Too Many Requests, whatever the password, without the password being checked. Attempts during a lock do not extend it.
Failures are counted by username, whether or not the account exists, and apart for OS accounts, LDAP accounts and the admin account. Spellings that may reach one account count as one: case, spaces at either end and repeated spaces, full-width forms and invisible characters make no difference, and for an OS account neither does a domain, so alice, DOMAIN\alice and alice@domain count together. A failure more than the period after the one before it starts the count again, and a good login clears it. A login that could not be checked (503 Service Unavailable) does not count.
An LDAP account also counts by the directory entry a username finds, so that other names for one account share its attempts. When they are used up, a login with another name answers 401 Unauthorized, as a wrong password does, without the password being checked.
Each login takes one of the username's attempts while it is being checked, so that logins sent at the same time cannot get more checks than the limit: one sent when all the attempts left are in use answers 429 Too Many Requests for one second, even with the right password.
Set the limits in config.yaml in the data directory, and restart the service:
jwt:
    lockout:
        max_failures: 3 # failed logins in a row that start a lock, at least 1
        period: 5m0s    # how long a failure counts with the next one, at least 1s
        duration: 5m0s  # how long a lock lasts, at least 1s

A value that is missing takes the default shown here, which is written to the file. One that cannot be used takes the default too, and logs a warning at each start until it is corrected. No setting turns the lockout off.
The counts are kept in memory, so restarting the service unlocks every username:
auth-server service restart

The auth-server keeps at most 10000 records of failures at a time: one for each username and one for each LDAP entry, so a failed LDAP login can take two. Past that, a new record takes the place of the oldest one that is neither locked nor being checked, whose count starts again, and the log says so at most once a minute. A lock is never dropped: while all 10000 are locked or being checked, a login with any other username answers 429 Too Many Requests too.

cli/edgehubagent.html.title: Advantech EdgeHub Device Agent Service (CLI)
cli/edgehubagent.html.body:
Advantech EdgeHub Agent Service (CLI)
Usage:
  edgehub-agent [flags]
  edgehub-agent [command]

Available Commands:
  app         Show and change which account owns each application
  conn        Apply connection setting
  help        Help about any command
  service     Manage service

Flags:
  -a, --address string                The IP address on which to listen for the --port port.
                                      If blank, 127.0.0.1: this host only, or all interfaces while
                                      LAN onboarding is on. Set to 0.0.0.0 for all IPv4 interfaces
                                      and :: for all IPv6 interfaces.
  -p, --port int                      The port on which to serve HTTPS with
                                      authentication and authorization.
                                      (default 8744)
      --tls-cert-file string          File containing the default x509 Certificate for HTTPS.
                                      (CA cert, if any, concatenated after server cert).
                                      If --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file are not provided,
                                      a self-signed certificate and key are generated for the public address
                                      and saved to the --tls-key-dir.
                                       (default "cert.crt")
      --tls-private-key-file string   File containing the default x509 private key
                                      matching --tls-cert-file.
                                       (default "key.pem")
      --tls-key-dir string            Location of --tls-cert-file and --tls-private-key-file
                                       (default "/etc/xdg/Advantech/.edgehub-agent/keys")
      --insecure-address string       The IP address on which to serve the --insecure-port.
                                      If blank, 127.0.0.1: this host only. Set to 0.0.0.0 for all IPv4
                                      interfaces and :: for all IPv6 interfaces.
      --insecure-port int             The port on which to serve plain HTTP, which does not encrypt
                                      passwords or tokens. Off by default. Set to 0 to disable.
      --jwt-auth-server-url string    Authentication Server URL
                                       (default "https://localhost:6443")
      --jwt-cert-file string          File containing the default x509 Certificate for JWT.
                                      (CA cert, if any, concatenated after server cert).
                                       (default "cert.crt")
      --jwt-cert-dir string           Location of --jwt-cert-file
                                       (default "/etc/xdg/Advantech/.edgehub-agent/keys/jwt")
      --jwt-check-interval duration   Duration that check and download JWT certificate
                                      from the authentication server. (default 5s)
      --config string                 Location of config files
                                       (default "/etc/xdg/Advantech/.edgehub-agent")
  -d, --debug                         enable debug output
  -h, --help                          help for edgehub-agent
      --version                       version for edgehub-agent

Use "edgehub-agent [command] --help" for more information about a command.

On Windows, edgehub-agent.exe runs with the rights of the user who starts it. Running the agent itself, the service commands, the app commands, and the conn commands that change the connection (conn with a setting, enable, disable, reset and rollback-key) need a command prompt opened with Run as administrator, as changing the settings through the portal needs an account in the Administrators group; they say so when they lack it. conn status, conn mac and the wsl commands run in an ordinary command prompt. While the agent is not running, conn mac needs an elevated prompt, and only an elevated conn status also tells whether a connection setting is stored, as only administrators may read the agent's settings.
On Linux, run edgehub-agent as root, for example with sudo: the agent's socket admits only root, and only root may read its data directory. As any other user, running the agent and the service, app and conn commands stop and say that they need root.
Data Directories tells where the agent keeps its data, who may use it, and how to restrict a directory given with --config, which the agent refuses to start on otherwise.
Plain HTTP is off by default. To turn it on, give --insecure-port, or server.http.port in the config file, a port other than 8789: that was its default, and it now turns plain HTTP off. The exception is a device with HTTPS off (server.https.port 0), where that port stays on, because a service must keep one of the two.

service command
Manage service

Usage:
  edgehub-agent service [flags]
  edgehub-agent service [command]

Available Commands:
  install     install service
  restart     restart service
  start       start service
  stop        stop service
  uninstall   uninstall service

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for service

Global Flags:
      --config string   Location of config files
                         (default "/etc/xdg/Advantech/.edgehub-agent")
  -d, --debug           enable debug output

Use "edgehub-agent service [command] --help" for more information about a command.


conn command
The device credential is set in the Dashboard or with POST /edgehub/api/conncfg; the conn command manages the stored one.
conn mac prints the MAC the device holds, the one GET /edgehub/api/macaddr returns; POST /edgehub/api/conncfg says when a connected device takes a new one. conn mac --all also lists the network adapters whose MAC a device credential may name, as that section describes: the wired ones first, then the wireless ones, each in ascending order, with (current) after the MAC the device holds, which is listed as other when it is none of them. On Windows an adapter whose MAC is overridden is listed by its burned-in MAC as well.
Apply connection setting

Usage:
  edgehub-agent conn [flags]
  edgehub-agent conn [command]

Available Commands:
  disable      Set connection to Disabled state
  enable       Set connection to Enabled state
  mac          Get MAC address for the connection
  reset        Reset connection settings
  rollback-key Re-encrypt the stored settings under the previous key, before a downgrade
  status       Get connection status

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for conn

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

  -d, --debug               enable debug output

Use "edgehub-agent conn [command] --help" for more information about a command.


app command
The agent hands an application credential only to the operating system account that owns the application's registration in the cloud. That is the account whose request made the cloud register the application, or, for a registration the cloud already had and no account on the device owned, the first account that asked for it: one registered in EdgeHub, one deleted in EdgeHub and registered again under the same name, which gets a new registration, or one whose first request got no answer. A request from any other account is refused with 403 Forbidden. On Windows the account is the Windows user the application runs as, SYSTEM included; on Linux it is the user ID, root included. A container counts as the account that runs its container engine: root for a rootful engine, the user for a rootless one, and in WSL 2 the Windows user who ran wsl setup for the distribution; the user ID inside the container does not count. On Linux an account whose user ID is from 61184 to 65519, the range systemd gives services with DynamicUser=yes their user IDs from, owns no application, and its requests are refused: systemd gives these user IDs to such services one after another, so whichever service held one next would receive the applications of the one before. Run such a service as a User= whose user ID is outside that range, DynamicUser=yes may stay, and a rootless container engine as a user outside it too. Before deleting a user, release its applications: its user ID may be given to the next user created. Administrators are bound like any other account.
The agent keeps these records for its own device registration. Connected to the cloud of another site, it starts there with none, and finds its records again when it connects back. A record names the registration it is about, so when the cloud registers a name again, the record of the earlier registration stays beside the new one's. Each record also keeps its site, the MQTT broker host the device credential named when the record was made: two clouds can give a device the same devId, and the app commands by name act only on the records of the site the agent is connected to. The owner of a registration is decided by its uuid alone, so the owners keep their registrations when a cloud moves its broker.
The app commands need an elevated command prompt, or root on Linux, and a running agent:
edgehub-agent app owners
edgehub-agent app assign --type SCADA --name plant-a --account "DOMAIN\user"
edgehub-agent app release --type SCADA --name plant-a
edgehub-agent app release --uuid 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000

owners lists the applications that have an owner, one line for each registration, with its site. assign makes an account the owner of an application in place of the account that owned it, also before the application is registered: whichever registration the cloud holds under the name when the next request at this site reaches it goes to that account. A later assignment of the name replaces an earlier one. The account is a user name or a SID on Windows, and a user name or user ID on Linux; app assign --help says where to find the account a program runs as. A group cannot own an application: a program runs as one account, never as a group. On Linux neither can a user ID from 61184 to 65519, the range systemd gives services with DynamicUser=yes their user IDs from. On Windows the account has to be one the system can look up: a user, SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, or a virtual account such as NT SERVICE\name. Give a user of the device as COMPUTERNAME\user: a name without a domain also finds a domain account when the device has no user of that name. A service's account can be given as sc.exe qc prints it, LocalSystem and .\user included. A domain account cannot be assigned while no domain controller answers. release removes the records of an application at this site, of each of its registrations, and each registration goes to the next account that asks for it. Both take the name in any letter case. release --uuid removes the record of one registration made at any site, such as one of another cloud or one the cloud has deleted.
An application registration belongs to the operating system account whose
process made the cloud create it, or, for one the cloud already had that no
account here owned, to the first account that asked for it; the agent hands
its credential to that account only. A container acts as the account that
runs its engine. A registration the cloud creates anew under a known name,
with a new uuid, is nobody's until an account asks for it; the record of the
earlier one stays. Records are kept per device registration of the agent, so
they follow the cloud the agent is connected to, and each keeps its site, the
broker the device credential named; by name, these commands reach the records
of the site the agent is connected to. They need administrator rights and a
running agent.

Usage:
  edgehub-agent app [command]

Available Commands:
  assign      Make an account the owner of an application, in place of any owner it had
  owners      List the applications that have an owner, and the account of each
  release     Remove the owners of an application

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for app

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

  -d, --debug               enable debug output

Use "edgehub-agent app [command] --help" for more information about a command.

Make an account the owner of an application, in place of any owner it had.
The assignment is to the name, in any letter case, at the site the agent is
connected to, and replaces an earlier assignment of it there: the next request
at that site that reaches a registration of the name takes that registration
for the account, whoever held it. Records of the name's other registrations
stay.

Usage:
  edgehub-agent app assign [flags]

Flags:
      --account string   the account a program of the application runs as, not a group:
                         DOMAIN\user, COMPUTERNAME\user, SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE,
                         NT SERVICE\name or a SID. To find it:
                           a user's program: whoami, run as that user
                           a service: SERVICE_START_NAME in sc.exe qc , as printed
                           a running program: (Get-Process  -IncludeUserName).UserName
                           a WSL 2 container: the Windows user who ran wsl setup in its distribution
  -h, --help             help for assign
      --name string      the application name
      --type string      the application type: EdgeLink, SCADA or Application

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

  -d, --debug               enable debug output

On Linux the --account flag reads:
      --account string   the account a program of the application runs as: a user name or uid.
                         To find it, while the program runs:
                           a program: ps -o uid= -p 
                           a systemd service: ps -o uid= -p $(systemctl show -p MainPID --value ),
                             with systemctl --user for a user service
                           a container: root under a rootful engine, the user who runs a rootless one
                         The uids 61184 to 65519, which systemd gives to services with DynamicUser=yes,
                         own no application: run the program, or the engine of its container, as a user
                         outside them.

Remove the records of an application at the site the agent is connected to,
in any letter case and of each of its registrations, or, with --uuid, the
record of one registration made at any site. Each registration then goes to
the next account that asks for it.

Usage:
  edgehub-agent app release [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help          help for release
      --name string   the application name
      --type string   the application type: EdgeLink, SCADA or Application
      --uuid string   the uuid of one registration, as app owners lists it

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

  -d, --debug               enable debug output


wsl command (Windows only)
Containers in WSL 2 on a Windows device, run by Docker or Podman in a WSL distribution or in a Podman machine, reach the agent through a relay in that distribution. edgehub-agent.exe wsl setup installs the relay as a systemd service that starts with the distribution. Run it once for each distribution a container engine runs in, and again after upgrading the agent, to update the relay. Docker Desktop is not supported.
Every wsl command takes the distribution's name, as wsl --list shows it, in --distro:
edgehub-agent.exe wsl setup --distro Ubuntu-22.04

For a Podman machine, pass the machine's name or its distribution name, for example --distro podman-machine-default.
Before running setup:

The distribution runs systemd, as Ubuntu installed with wsl --install does by default. Otherwise add systemd=true under [boot] in the distribution's /etc/wsl.conf, run wsl --terminate , and start the distribution again. A Podman machine runs systemd.
The container engine serves its API socket in the distribution. Docker does while it runs; rootful Podman does once podman.socket is enabled, with sudo systemctl enable --now podman.socket. A Podman machine does.
The agent service is running.
The command runs as the Windows user the distribution belongs to, in an ordinary command prompt. An elevated prompt that runs as another administrator account sees that account's distributions instead. The agent service cannot install the relay itself, because a WSL distribution belongs to a user.

setup asks the agent for a relay key of the Windows user who runs it, which the agent issues on the first request and keeps where only administrators and SYSTEM can read it, and installs it in the distribution. Every caller the relay passes on counts as that Windows user, as all the WSL distributions of a Windows user run in one virtual machine of that user. setup checks the distribution before it replaces anything, and changes nothing if a check fails. At the end it runs a short-lived container to confirm that the relay identifies containers; if that fails, the new relay stays installed and setup says what failed. status shows the relay in the distribution and what the agent sees of relays, which GET /edgehub/api/wsl/status also reports; remove stops the relay and removes what setup installed.
A container that provisions an application credential through the agent needs the distribution's /run/edgehub directory mounted, read-only is enough, and two labels set when the container is created. Applications that follow the EdgeHub Connect SDK documentation read the same type and name from two environment variables, which the example sets too:
docker run -v /run/edgehub:/run/edgehub:ro \
  --label com.advantech.edgehub.app.type=Application \
  --label com.advantech.edgehub.app.name=line-3-sensor \
  -e EDGEHUB_APP_TYPE=Application \
  -e EDGEHUB_APP_NAME=line-3-sensor \
  

com.advantech.edgehub.app.type is Application, EdgeLink or SCADA, and com.advantech.edgehub.app.name is the name of the application the container provisions. The agent allows the container exactly that type and name, in the same letter case, and only an application the Windows user who set up the relay may have, as the app command above describes: a request for any other, or from a container without the labels, is refused with 403 Forbidden. Only the labels carry authority; the environment variables only tell the application what to ask for. If the container engine does not answer when the relay looks up the labels, or the relay cannot reach the agent, the request is refused with 503 Service Unavailable and can be retried. The same options work with podman run, also from Windows against a Podman machine.
Set up the relay that lets containers in a WSL2 distro reach this agent

Usage:
  edgehub-agent wsl [command]

Available Commands:
  remove      Stop the relay in a WSL distro and remove what setup installed
  setup       Install or update the relay in the WSL distro a container engine runs in
  status      Show the relay in a WSL distro, and what the agent sees of relays

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for wsl

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

  -d, --debug               enable debug output

Use "edgehub-agent wsl [command] --help" for more information about a command.

Install or update the relay in the WSL distro a container engine runs in

Usage:
  edgehub-agent wsl setup [flags]

Flags:
      --distro string   the WSL distro, or podman machine, the container engine runs in
      --dry-run         print what setup would install, without installing anything
  -h, --help            help for setup

Global Flags:
      --config PathString   Location of config files

  -d, --debug               enable debug output

status and remove take the same --distro flag, without --dry-run.


LAN onboarding
LAN onboarding lets a utility on the local network, such as the EdgeHub utility, find this device over mDNS and register it with EdgeHub without logging in to the device. It is off by default: the agent does not advertise itself, has no initial code, and answers 404 Not Found on POST /edgehub/api/initialcode, POST /edgehub/api/device/challenge and POST /edgehub/api/device/register. Its HTTPS port listens on this host only, unless server.https.address names another address, and other hosts reach the agent through the portal.
To turn it on, stop the service, add this to config.yaml in the agent's data directory, and start the service again. A running agent rewrites that file and reads the setting only as it starts, so change the file while the service is stopped:
device:
  lanOnboarding: true

The initial code is broadcast in plain text. While LAN onboarding is on, anyone who can hear mDNS can register a device that has no stored connection configuration, so turn it on only on a trusted network, and only while it is needed. Set the value back to false, or remove it, to turn LAN onboarding off.
While LAN onboarding is on, the agent's HTTPS port listens on all interfaces when server.https.address is blank, for the utility to reach it. A client on another host reaches only the device challenge and registration there, and gets 403 Forbidden for any other request, on any address the agent listens on; programs on this host and requests through the portal are served as before. Plain HTTP stays on this host only when server.http.address is blank.
When an application is refused
An application the agent refuses its credential gets 403 Forbidden; an application built on the EdgeHub Connect SDK reports EHC_PROVISION_ERROR_NOT_AUTHORIZED, and its error text holds the agent's reason, which the agent also writes to its log. Asking again gets the same answer until the cause is removed; then restart the application, or let it ask again. A caller the agent failed to identify, the second group under the caller could not be identified below, gets 503 Service Unavailable instead, which the SDK reports as EHC_PROVISION_ERROR_AGENT_UNAVAILABLE, with the reason too. By the reason, where ... stands for the part that differs from case to case:

... "...": the application belongs to another account on this device
First check that the type and name the message starts with are the application's own: a program that asks for another application's name gets this answer too, and has to ask for its own name instead. If they are its own, the application runs as another operating system account than the one that owns its registration: for example, it was first started as another user, or another program asked for the same name first. An administrator sees the owner with edgehub-agent app owners. Run the application as that account or, once sure the application is the one meant to have the registration, have an administrator assign it to the account the application runs as with edgehub-agent app assign; edgehub-agent app assign --help says how to find that account. An assignment takes the application from its current owner.

this container is deployed as ... and may provision only that application
The application in the container asks for another application than the one the container's labels name, which the message gives. If the labels are right, have the application ask for the type and name the message gives. If the labels are wrong, create the container again with the labels com.advantech.edgehub.app.type and com.advantech.edgehub.app.name set to the application's type and name, in the same letter case.

this container was deployed without an application identity
The container has no labels naming its application. Create the container again with the labels com.advantech.edgehub.app.type and com.advantech.edgehub.app.name set to the application's type and name, in the same letter case.

this endpoint serves host processes; a container provisions through /run/edgehub/app.sock
A container reached the agent's own socket, which serves programs on the host only. Mount /run/edgehub into the container instead, read-only is enough, and ask through /run/edgehub/app.sock.

uid ...: this account can own no application: systemd gives the uids 61184 to 65519 to services with DynamicUser=yes, one after another; ... (Linux)
The application runs as a user ID that systemd gives to services with DynamicUser=yes, and may give to another service later; for an application in a container, the user ID is that of the user who runs the container engine. Run the application, or the engine of its container, as a user whose user ID is outside that range. For a systemd system service, an administrator adds User= naming such a user to the service's unit, DynamicUser=yes may stay, then runs systemctl daemon-reload and restarts the service. Should the application already belong to another account, the next request is refused for that reason, as the first entry describes.

the caller could not be identified: ..., or the account of the caller could not be read: ...
The agent could not tell which account is asking; the rest of the message says why. These reasons are what the agent found out about the caller, and get 403 Forbidden:

the caller opened the pipe anonymously; ... (Windows): the program opened the agent's pipe without letting the agent read its account. Open the pipe at the SECURITY_IDENTIFICATION impersonation level or above, as the EdgeHub Connect SDK does.
in a container of a runtime this agent does not know (Linux): the agent tells apart the containers of Docker and Podman only. Run the application in a Docker or Podman container, or on the host.
outside this agent's pid namespace (Linux): the agent cannot see the application's process, as when the agent itself runs in a container. An administrator installs the agent on the host.
the container's application labels are longer than any application name (WSL 2): the relay found labels too long to name an application. Create the container again with the labels set to the application's type and name.

Any other reason means the agent failed to identify the caller, and gets 503 Service Unavailable: asking again may succeed. In WSL 2, a container whose relay edgehub-agent.exe wsl setup installed from an earlier agent gets 403 Forbidden for these too, until wsl setup runs again.

the peer exited before it could be identified, the process at the peer's pid does not hold the connection, or pidfd_open: no such process: the process that connected to the agent exited, or handed its connection to another process and closed its own, while the agent was identifying it. The agent identifies the process that connects, so that process has to keep its connection, and stay alive, until it has the answer. If the application does this every time, change how it connects.
A reason that ends in operation not permitted or permission denied, every time: a restriction keeps the program that identifies callers from making the call the reason names, such as a system call filter that denies pidfd_send_signal or pidfd_open. On a Linux device, look at the agent's service, such as a SystemCallFilter= in its unit; for a container in WSL 2, look at the relay's service in that distribution, edgehub-wsl-relay.service, not at the agent on Windows.
Any other reason names the read or the system call that failed, in the agent or, for a container in WSL 2, in the relay in its distribution. If it returns, an administrator removes the cause it names.

The agent's log has the same reason as the application.

applications are provisioned through the agent's local pipe or socket, never over the network
The request came over the network. Applications ask from the device itself, through \\.\pipe\edgehub_app on Windows or /run/edgehub/app.sock on Linux, as the EdgeHub Connect SDK does.

Appendix
Server-Sent Events (SSE)
Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a server push technology enabling a client to receive automatic updates from a server via HTTP connection. The Server-Sent Events EventSource API is standardized as part of HTML5 by the W3C.
Receiving events from the server
Our SSE APIs require token to access the data from the server. You can Login with OS account to get the token (token field from the response body), or using Secure and HttpOnly cookies (if available).
// Open a connection
const evtSource = new EventSource("/THE_SSE_API?token=", { withCredentials: true } );

// Handle events
evtSource.addEventListener(, (event) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
  // process your data
});
